purpose: Interpret observed OCR/visual clues, propose geographic lookups and support candidate ranking.
source_age_notes: CTT-derived postcode/address associations use data dated 2020-04-09.
The Spanish kilometre-marker community document ends in 2023; infrastructure may have changed.
Guide maps read from infographics describe approximate tendencies, not verified boundaries.
The selected physical facts were reviewed in the supplied notes; this extraction is not a new fact check of every upstream source.

selection.primary: Readable identifiers and distinctive, practical country/city/area separators.
selection.secondary: Useful regional physical clues, or small details that require a close crop.
selection.context: Broad or historical fallback tendencies; weak support only.
excluded: Challenge panorama locations, answers or evaluation-derived priors
Raw video inventories/transcripts and unverified auto-caption facts
Unverified tax-ID regional rules and installation-code guesses
Address-frequency percentages used as image/location probabilities

rules: Observe appearance/text before retrieving its geographic implications.
not_visible, unreadable, other and skipped questions supply no location evidence.
Explicit international prefixes override national-format matches; keep the full OCR token.
Full place/code lookup precedes topographic or toponym tendencies.
A landmark/area coordinate is not camera GPS; retain its geographic extent and uncertainty.
Deduplicate the same object across views; group related clues and copied sources before weighting.
Give scene/architecture/vegetation hints bounded influence and retain alternative countries.
Keep the generic KB fixed between panoramas; every run starts with fresh observations and candidates.
Human questions have at most four explicit options; choose candidate-separating visible features only.
source_dependence: LearnableMeta often repeats Plonk It; do not count their agreement twice.
Geomastr images and Rainbolt quotes are supporting illustrations/methods, not extra independent observations.

pt_postal_zones.purpose: Coarse regional fallback for a verified Portuguese postcode.
caveats: Postal regions differ from administrative boundaries.
Full-code gazetteer lookup is more specific.
9 covers both Madeira and the Azores.

entries.postal_region: City of Lisbon (+ bits of Oeiras, Odivelas, Loures)
Lisbon region outside the city, Santarém, Oeste, Setúbal peninsula

pt_phone_areas.purpose: Longest-prefix match after Portuguese number/country classification.
caveats: Numbering-area names and the district of the named town are not coverage polygons.
Advertised contact numbers can belong to remote offices.
The source has unverified coverage wording for 21; rely on Lisboa as its area name.
Horta/Angra/Ponta Delgada area names do not verify exclusive island boundaries.

pt_municipal_codes.purpose: Validate a contextual three-letter postal/trail municipal code.
caveats: Require a postal, trail or clearly identified municipal-code context.
The municipality is an area, not a camera coordinate.

es_postal_provinces.purpose: Province of the first two digits after country disambiguation.
caveats: All 01–52 prefixes also occur in French postal space.
Preserve leading zeros.
Ceuta and Melilla are autonomous cities.

es_phone_areas.purpose: Longest listed geographic prefix, after country and service/mobile classification.
caveats: Unprefixed 91/92/93/96 can be Portuguese mobiles.
952 and 956 have Melilla/Ceuta exceptions.
Do not extrapolate unlisted geographic prefixes or infer operator geography from a mobile.

es_regional_roads.purpose: Region/province candidates for a full observed Spanish road identifier.
caveats: A alone is national/Andalucía/Aragón/Álava/CyL; CA is Cantabria/Cádiz; GI is Girona/Gipuzkoa.
HU is Huesca/Huelva; LP is Lleida/La Palma; CV is Valenciana or local camino vecinal; CM is CLM or a Salamanca local code.
M, MA and Ma mean different things: Madrid, Málaga and Mallorca.
L/LL and several provincial prefixes are disputed; verify the full route in maps.
The listing is descriptive notation, not an executable regex whitelist.

entries.provincial_designations_as_source: AL, ALP (Almería) · CA (Cádiz) · CO, CP, CV (Córdoba) · GR (Granada) · HU, HF, HV and H (Huelva; sources disagree) · JA, JV, JF (Jaén) · MA (Málaga) · SE (Sevilla)
HU, HU-V (Huesca) · TE, TE-V (Teruel) · CV, Z, ZP (Zaragoza) · CHE (Ebro water authority)
GC, TF, LZ, FV, LP, HI, GM (+CV)
AB · CR · CU, CUV · GU · TO
AV, AV-P · BU, BU-P, BU-V · LE · P, PP · SA, DSA (+SA-CV, CV, CM tier 3) · SG, SG-V, SG-P · SO, SO-P · VA, VP · ZA, ZA-P
BV, BP (Barcelona) · GIV, GIP (Girona) · LV, LP (and L) (Lleida; Plonk It writes "LL") · TV, TP (Tarragona)
AC + DP/CP (A Coruña) · LU + LU-P (Lugo) · OU (Ourense) · PO + EP (Pontevedra)

es_city_access_roads.purpose: Specific city-access/ring-road identifiers to check against map geometry.
caveats: Slash/range notation is copied as a shorthand and must not be expanded into invented roads.
VG has a Vigo/Vitoria-Gasteiz collision; keep the exact number.

fr_departments.purpose: Department-code names and regions for a resolved French postal or institutional identifier.
caveats: Corsican postal prefix 20 requires full-code lookup to decide 2A/2B.
Modern plate departments are owner-chosen.
A postal prefix can identify a neighbouring delivering post office.

regional_transport_brands.purpose: Regional support from a readable full brand on transport infrastructure.
caveats: Moving buses/coaches can leave the service region.
EMT and bare TER are excluded because they are not uniquely regional.

fr_regional_newspapers.purpose: Conservative regional support from contextual newspaper names.
caveats: Source coverage is a historical distribution association, not exclusivity or a camera location.
Defunct/merged Le Havre titles, L’Écho du Centre and uncertain Nord éclair/Libération Champagne were excluded.
Both Centre Presse associations are retained.

entries.title: Ouest-France
entries.coverage_as_source: Bretagne, Normandie, Pays de la Loire

rules.observation: A legible place, street, landmark or business name in its surrounding sign text.
rules.action: Resolve exact names and aliases in panoloc.names; keep all ambiguous matches and verify the sign context.
exceptions: A direction arrow names a destination, not the camera location.
Advertisements, visiting vehicles and pictures may mention distant places.
An area or landmark coordinate is not camera GPS.

rules.observation: A contextual seven-digit postcode written as four digits, a separator and three digits.
rules.action: Normalise spacing and OCR-supported separators, then call Names.postcode(); use pt_postal_zones only as a coarse fallback.
exceptions: A four-digit prefix can cover more than one municipality.
Postal coordinates describe an area; do not treat a centroid as a camera.
Require address context before interpreting bare numbers.

rules.observation: A contextual five-digit postcode whose first two digits are 01 through 52.
rules.action: Keep both ES and FR until language, an explicit country marker or locality resolves the collision; use es_postal_provinces after resolving ES.
exceptions: Prefixes 01–52 overlap French codes.
Years, prices and telephone fragments are not postcodes.
The third digit 0 suggests a provincial capital, not a camera position.

rules.observation: A contextual five-digit French postal address with a commune name; metropolitan prefixes extend to 95.
rules.action: Resolve the complete code with Names.postcode(); after resolving FR, use fr_departments for the postal prefix.
exceptions: Prefixes 01–52 overlap Spain.
The prefix can identify a neighbouring delivering post office.
Corsican postal codes use 20; resolve the full code rather than inventing a 2A/2B split.
CEDEX and special-recipient codes need gazetteer lookup.

rules.observation: A complete phone number includes +351/00351, +34/0034 or +33/0033.
rules.action: Parse the complete phone token first: 351→PT, 34→ES, 33→FR. An explicit prefix takes precedence over all national-format guesses.
exceptions: The telephone registration country need not be the camera country.
Never match another country’s national regex inside an explicitly prefixed number.

rules.observation: A nine-digit Portuguese fixed-line number begins with 2; 21 and 22 are the two-digit area prefixes.
rules.action: After country disambiguation, use the longest matching pt_phone_areas prefix to propose a numbering area.
exceptions: The area name is not a verified municipality boundary.
Businesses and vehicles may advertise a remote head office.
Preserve OCR alternatives instead of adding missing digits.

rules.observation: A nine-digit Spanish number falls in a geographic 8/9 range listed in es_phone_areas.
rules.action: Resolve the country first, exclude service ranges, then use the longest listed geographic prefix.
exceptions: Unprefixed 91/92/93/96 numbers can be Portuguese mobiles.
900/901/902 and other service ranges are not provincial evidence.
956 is shared with Ceuta and 952 with Melilla.

rules.observation: A French fixed-line number starts 01, 02, 03, 04 or 05.
rules.action: Use as a historical regional hint only: 01 Île-de-France; 02 north-west; 03 north-east; 04 south-east; 05 south-west. Combine with independent text.
exceptions: Since 2023-01-01, existing and newly assigned metropolitan numbers can use a different region’s prefix.
Avoid deriving a department from the following two digits without independent evidence.
Telemarketing prefixes and remote head offices carry no reliable local position.

rules.observation: A mobile, VoIP, freephone or national service number is legible.
rules.action: Use a verified international prefix for country support only; supply no regional support from a mobile or service number.
exceptions: PT mobiles commonly use 91/92/93/96, overlapping Spanish geographic numbers.
FR 06/07 are mobile and 09 is non-geographic.
ES 6/7 are mostly mobile; special ranges require classification.

rules.observation: Câmara Municipal de X, Município de X, Junta de Freguesia de X or União das Freguesias de X e Y.
rules.action: Read and geocode X; municipal/parish names usually narrow the area far more than building style.
exceptions: Check whether the wording labels the current office, a destination or an advertisement.
Repeated parish names need municipality context.

rules.observation: Ayuntamiento, Ajuntament, Concello or Udala followed by a locality.
rules.action: Read the locality, including on vado/no-parking permits, and resolve it in the name index.
exceptions: Language and institutional terms must be read in context.
A common town or street name remains ambiguous.

rules.observation: Mairie de X, Hôtel de Ville or a readable département name on fixed infrastructure.
rules.action: Extract the commune or department name and resolve it with the name index.
exceptions: Mairie or Hôtel de Ville alone gives country support, not a commune.
Department logos need a reliable reading; do not invent their text.

rules.observation: A three-letter code occurs in a postal designation or a PR/GR hiking-trail identifier.
rules.action: Validate the code in pt_municipal_codes, then resolve the municipality; combine the trail number with local trail data when available.
exceptions: Three arbitrary capitals on a shop sign are not necessarily a municipal code.
The number alone is not geographically unique.
A municipality or trail is an area, not a camera location.

rules.observation: A Portuguese hunting-zone sign includes a process number such as 3475-ICNF or an older DGF suffix.
rules.action: Query or prefetch the ICNF hunting-zone polygons by num_def; intersect the returned area with other candidates.
exceptions: The polygon may span an estate or an entire municipality.
Use zone-name/type context to validate the number.
The AFN/DGRF suffix variants in the research are unverified guesses and are not recognition rules here.

rules.observation: IP or IC is legible in a road identifier; an EN/N, ER, EM or CM identifier has Portuguese sign context.
rules.action: Resolve the observed route in map data; use the number and any kilometre marker to narrow its segment.
exceptions: Bare A/N numbers also occur in France.
EM/CM numbers repeat geographically.
Portuguese CM and Spanish CM identifiers need country context.

rules.observation: A regional Spanish road identifier is legible, such as CL-517, EX-206, AS-II or AG-55.
rules.action: Use es_regional_roads and its collision list, then resolve the complete designation in road data.
exceptions: A, CA, GI, HU, LP, CV, C and CM are ambiguous.
Hyphens can disappear in OCR or on some signs.
Do not resolve a disputed prefix to one province without another clue.

rules.observation: A complete city-access or ring-road designation is readable.
rules.action: Use es_city_access_roads as a shortlist, then verify the actual road in maps.
exceptions: The source uses abbreviated ranges; these do not assert every number in a range exists.
VG-11/20 points to Vigo while VG-21/31/41 points to Vitoria-Gasteiz.
A direction sign can point towards a road some distance away.

rules.observation: A yellow D/RD cartouche, cyan M cartouche, or contextual Corsican T-road identifier is readable.
rules.action: D/RD→departmental network; M→metropolitan network; T→Corsica. Resolve the entire road with department/commune context.
exceptions: D-road numbers repeat across departments.
Bare A/N fits Portugal too.
Spanish T-11 at Reus can resemble a Corsican T identifier if a hyphen is lost.
Cartouche colour without readable letters may be misleading.

rules.observation: A road identifier and a kilometre, hectometre or PR marker are both readable.
rules.action: Locate the road and marker in available map/reference data, then estimate the camera offset using visible geometry.
exceptions: The road number must first be disambiguated.
A French PR is not guaranteed to equal a kilometre distance.
Open marker-coordinate coverage was not established by the research.

rules.observation: A complete contextual domain suffix or regional-government URL is readable.
rules.action: Use .pt/.es/.fr as country support, .gal for Galicia, .eus for Basque-language areas and .cat for Catalan-language areas.
exceptions: A business domain may serve several regions or countries.
.eus and Catalan language cross the France–Spain border.
Avoid classifying a short fragment that is not visibly a URL.

rules.observation: A readable full regional transport brand occurs on a fixed stop, station or local service sign.
rules.action: Look up the full brand in regional_transport_brands; verify the locality or stop name next.
exceptions: A coach can travel outside its service area.
A generic acronym such as EMT or TER is not uniquely regional.
Brand geography is a service area, not a camera point.

rules.observation: A legible regional newspaper title occurs on a kiosk, dispenser or shop awning.
rules.action: Use fr_regional_newspapers for a department/region shortlist; corroborate with local signs.
exceptions: Newspapers travel and shops can sell more than one regional title.
Old signage may survive a closure or merger.
Centre Presse has two distinct local associations; preserve both.

rules.observation: Words Rua, Travessa, Largo, Câmara, Freguesia; combinations such as ã/õ, lh/nh and -ção/-ções.
rules.action: Read the full name before using language as a regional hint; retain every matching place.
exceptions: ç and many accents are shared with French or Catalan.
Galician Rúa may lose its accent in OCR.

rules.observation: Words Calle, Ayuntamiento, del/los and combinations such as ñ and -ción.
rules.action: Read the full name before using language as a regional hint; retain every matching place.
exceptions: Common individual words and letters are shared by other languages.

rules.observation: Words Rue, Impasse, Allée, Chemin, Mairie and combinations such as œ and du/des.
rules.action: Read the full name before using language as a regional hint; retain every matching place.
exceptions: A single accent or the word avenue is not a French-only signal.

rules.observation: Rúa, Concello, Xunta, unha, praza or igrexa in a coherent Galician reading.
rules.action: Read the full name before using language as a regional hint; retain every matching place.
exceptions: The landscape and some vocabulary resemble northern Portugal.
An isolated x or missing accent is insufficient.

rules.observation: Carrer, Ajuntament, plaça, l·l or a coherent Catalan/Valencian text line.
rules.action: Read the full name before using language as a regional hint; retain every matching place.
exceptions: Catalan and the Senyera occur on both sides of the border.
An isolated ç is shared with Portuguese and French.

rules.observation: Coherent Basque text with tx/tz and terms such as kalea, karrika or udala.
rules.action: Read the full name before using language as a regional hint; retain every matching place.
exceptions: Basque and the ikurriña cross the border.
Kalea favours Spain and karrika favours France; corroborate before choosing a country.

rules.observation: Straed, Hent or Plasenn with c'h/zh in a coherent Breton line.
rules.action: Read the full name before using language as a regional hint; retain every matching place.
exceptions: A single short word or flag on a visitor’s vehicle is weaker.

rules.observation: A coherent Mirandese line, for example Miranda de l Douro, Bumioso, or l/ls with initial lh-.
rules.action: Read the full name before using language as a regional hint; retain every matching place.
exceptions: Portuguese and Spanish share many words; require several consistent cues.

rules.observation: Coherent Corsican text with chj/ghj, -u endings or carrughju alongside French.
rules.action: Read the full name before using language as a regional hint; retain every matching place.
exceptions: The language resembles Italian; corroborate with T roads, a full postcode or local names.

rules.observation: A blue P/EU band on the left and a yellow date band on the right.
rules.action: Support Portugal; read character groups separately with OCR.
exceptions: Older Portuguese plate designs carry the band; its absence never excludes PT.
Older registrations can have a replacement plate with no yellow band.
A visiting car can be registered abroad.

rules.observation: Blue bands at both ends, an F on the left and a department/logo on the right; AA-123-AA when readable.
rules.action: Support French registration; use plate format and F rather than colour alone.
exceptions: Italian plates also have blue bands at both ends.
The owner freely chooses the right-band department, so it is weak regional evidence.
A visiting car is not local proof.

rules.observation: A blue E/EU band on the left and four digits followed by three consonants.
rules.action: Support Spanish registration; use a readable E or character grouping.
exceptions: Left-band-only white plates also occur in Portugal.
Modern Spanish plates contain no province information.
A visiting car is not local proof.

rules.observation: A red CTT box with the horse-and-rider logo or correio wording; a blue Correio Azul box.
rules.action: Support Portugal; seek readable postal or nearby street text.
exceptions: Colour without a logo or postal context is weaker.
A decorative object is not necessarily a working post box.

rules.observation: A yellow Correos post box with a crown-and-horn logo.
rules.action: Support Spain; use the logo to distinguish La Poste.
exceptions: Yellow alone supports both Spain and France.

rules.observation: A yellow or heritage-brown La Poste box with a readable La Poste label or bird/arrow logo.
rules.action: Support France; use the label or logo to distinguish Correos.
exceptions: Yellow alone supports both Spain and France.

rules.observation: The identifiable Multibanco MB mark on an ATM or shop sticker.
rules.action: Support Portugal and inspect nearby shop/street names.
exceptions: Two generic letters MB without the logo are insufficient.

rules.observation: Small white limestone paving cubes, especially black-and-white patterned calçada.
rules.action: Support Portugal within the PT/ES/FR search scope; use local signs to narrow further.
exceptions: Some Spanish places use similar paving.
Granite setts and generic concrete pavers are not this feature.
Do not count the same paving twice across overlapping views.

rules.observation: Black curve boards with clearly yellow arrows.
rules.action: Support Portugal within PT/ES/FR.
exceptions: Confirm actual colours in a readable crop.
Blue/white chevrons occur in both France and Spain.
Similar designs exist outside the allowed country set.

rules.observation: A round white delineator with a pointed/conical top and an encircling grey or red reflective band.
rules.action: Support France; compare the round form and band, not whiteness alone.
exceptions: Rare wedge variants resemble Portugal.
Geomastr’s diagonal-black-band example is disputed and is not a French rule here.

rules.observation: A thin white wedge with a black band and small white reflector, or a flat post with a wide white reflector.
rules.action: Support Portugal conservatively and check an independent separator.
exceptions: Some French wedge types are similar.
Portuguese yellow/orange delineators occur on the left of one-way carriageways.
Portuguese and Spanish examples overlap substantially.

rules.observation: A hollow white delineator with a black band, yellow/orange rectangular reflector and possibly two white dots behind.
rules.action: Support Spain conservatively outside the Portuguese one-way-carriageway exception.
exceptions: PT motorway examples can look the same.
Viewing the opposite face changes reflector appearance.

rules.observation: Clearly red or yellow reflectors on a guardrail.
rules.action: Red favours PT; yellow favours ES. Combine with another road clue.
exceptions: AP-15 Navarra has red reflectors.
No visible reflector is missing evidence and does not prove France.

rules.observation: A readable red-bordered traffic sign whose red reaches its outer edge.
rules.action: Support Spain only when a close crop resolves the edge.
exceptions: PT/FR usually have a thin outer white rim.
Compression, glare and distant crops can erase a white rim.

rules.observation: A clearly resolved pedestrian-crossing sign with eight stripes.
rules.action: Support Spain when the stripes can actually be counted.
exceptions: PT/FR commonly use five stripes.
A 1024-pixel view often cannot resolve the pictogram; request a closer crop.

rules.observation: Concrete ladder-like poles with conspicuously tall rectangular openings.
rules.action: Support Portugal with another independent clue.
exceptions: Other countries use concrete ladder poles too.
A generic pole silhouette is insufficient.

rules.observation: A clearly visible small blue utility plate on a wooden or metal pole.
rules.action: Support France; read the label if possible.
exceptions: Generic blue stickers are weaker than an identifiable utility plate.

rules.observation: A white marker with a diagonally cut coloured left panel, or a Portuguese black/yellow-base stone marker.
rules.action: Read its road identifier and kilometre number with OCR.
exceptions: Shape/colour alone does not locate a road segment.
Use actual lettering to disambiguate similar markers.

rules.observation: A white borne with a yellow D-road or red N-road rounded cap.
rules.action: Read the road number, PR and department context.
exceptions: Old caps can survive road reclassification.
The department is still needed to disambiguate D numbers.

rules.observation: Red/white hunting-zone signs, especially readable ZONA DE CAÇA wording.
rules.action: Read the zone name and process number; use the ICNF area lookup.
exceptions: A red-white-red rectangle alone does not establish its precise legal meaning.
Do not infer no-hunting versus hunting-zone status solely from colour.

rules.observation: COTO … CAZA wording or a contextual black/white hunting-boundary plate.
rules.action: Read the place/provincial designation; use it as area support.
exceptions: Regional code formats vary.
A generic diagonal black/white object is not a hunting sign.

rules.observation: White chimney tops with intricate lattice work or rounded bodies capped by a small spire.
rules.action: Prioritise Algarve candidates and inspect nearby names/codes.
exceptions: One unusual chimney can be decorative or imported.
Whitewashed houses alone also occur in Spain.

rules.observation: Dense vineyard terraces with schist retaining walls along a river valley.
rules.action: Prioritise Douro candidates; compare terrain and river geometry.
exceptions: Terraced vineyards occur elsewhere; require the combination of vines, valley and schist.
Do not infer a town from the landscape alone.

rules.observation: A long narrow stone granary raised on pillars with slotted walls.
rules.action: Keep both northern Portugal and Galicia; use language, plaques or road furniture to separate them.
exceptions: Hórreos/espigueiros are shared across the border.
A cross on the gable is not a unique country separator.

rules.observation: A square wooden granary on four pillars with a pyramidal roof.
rules.action: Prioritise Asturias and nearby north-west Spanish alternatives.
exceptions: The form is not exclusively Asturian.
A rectangular six/eight-pillar panera is related, not an exact match.

rules.observation: Vines trained high on pergolas or trees around small field boundaries.
rules.action: Support Minho when combined with local text or other northern Portuguese clues.
exceptions: Agricultural forms cross borders.

rules.observation: Whitewashed walls with conspicuous blue or yellow painted bands around openings and wall edges.
rules.action: Support southern Portugal; check chimneys and readable signs.
exceptions: Plain whitewash is common in Andalucía and Extremadura.
A single painted building is insufficient.

rules.observation: Large unpainted grey blocks with conspicuously white mortar joints.
rules.action: Support northern PT; compare Galician alternatives with text.
exceptions: Bare block walls also occur in Galicia.
Modern construction and lighting can alter apparent mortar colour.

rules.observation: Small green pasture enclosures built from dark porous volcanic stone walls.
rules.action: Consider the Azores; seek island text, full postcodes or EDA identifiers.
exceptions: Volcanic materials occur in Madeira and the Canaries.
Black colour alone does not establish basalt.

rules.observation: A small ornate Holy Spirit chapel with distinctive crown decoration.
rules.action: Look up the chapel name; use its mapped landmark position as an area hypothesis.
exceptions: A landmark coordinate is not the camera point.
The architectural identification must be visible and specific.

rules.observation: Very steep stone-walled agricultural terraces, especially with visible banana plantations.
rules.action: Consider Madeira; check island roads, names and utility identifiers.
exceptions: Steep terraces alone are not unique.
Bananas or flowers alone do not establish the island.

rules.observation: Stone delineators with red reflectors, or mountain guardrails painted yellow and black.
rules.action: Support Madeira and inspect road identifiers such as VR1/ER101.
exceptions: Confirm actual delineators rather than generic boundary stones.
A painted guardrail alone is a regional hint.

rules.observation: A small triangular A-frame house with a steep thatched roof.
rules.action: Check Santana candidates and look for a named site.
exceptions: A replica or tourist display may be elsewhere.
Do not equate the house footprint with camera GPS.

rules.observation: A pale green plaque with white serif capitals and a notched top.
rules.action: Read the street name and resolve it within Porto.
exceptions: Colour alone is insufficient.
Use a locality corroboration before restricting all matches to Porto.

rules.observation: White stone street plaques with engraved borders and black serif capitals; tiled plaques or black plaques may also occur.
rules.action: Read the street name and compare Lisbon candidates.
exceptions: Plaques and azulejos are shared with other Portuguese towns.
The four-corner-bolt detail has limited source support and is not a decisive rule.

rules.observation: Grey square paving tiles with a clear four-petal flower/panot pattern.
rules.action: Prioritise Barcelona candidates and read adjacent street plaques.
exceptions: Generic patterned pavers are weaker.
Replicas and nearby municipalities remain possible.

rules.observation: An oval blue street plate in an ornate gilded frame, often bilingual.
rules.action: Read the street name and resolve it in Bilbao.
exceptions: A generic blue plaque is not this design.

rules.observation: A square marker topped by the red Madrid flag with white stars and a red M road prefix.
rules.action: Read the complete M-road and kilometre designation.
exceptions: M alone is not enough; French M roads are metropolitan.
Flags on movable objects have weaker local value.

rules.observation: The Spanish delineator form with a clearly green top.
rules.action: Support Extremadura; check EX road numbers or local names.
exceptions: Distinguish a painted top from vegetation, glare or a sticker.

rules.observation: An extra-tall regional road marker with Junta de Andalucía wording or a clear regional-government sign.
rules.action: Read the locality and road identifier.
exceptions: Green colour or marker height alone is weaker.
A-xxx numbers also occur in Aragón and Álava.

rules.observation: Extensive continuous white plastic agricultural greenhouses in an arid coastal landscape.
rules.action: Consider south-eastern Andalucía and corroborate with codes or names.
exceptions: Individual greenhouses occur throughout the search area.

rules.observation: A small square curve board with a red arrow on white.
rules.action: Support Murcia; check RM/MU road identifiers.
exceptions: Some reference galleries show red/white variants elsewhere; require the specific small-square form.

rules.observation: A large rounded-top marker with a readable Bizkaia logo or name.
rules.action: Use the readable province name and road/km identifier.
exceptions: Rounded shape without the logo is not sufficient.

rules.observation: Dark blue street plaque with a green frame, arched top and readable arrondissement/local text.
rules.action: Resolve the street name and arrondissement in Paris.
exceptions: A generic blue street plate is not a Paris identification.

rules.observation: A street plaque with the identifiable red slanted fleur-de-lis emblem.
rules.action: Read the street name and resolve it in Lille.
exceptions: A decorative fleur-de-lis on another object is weaker.

rules.observation: An imperial-domed bell tower covered in decorative glazed tiles.
rules.action: Prioritise Franche-Comté and look for church/commune names.
exceptions: Onion spires and plain domes are broader architectural forms.
A single landmark still requires identification.

rules.observation: A coherent historic streetscape of bright orange brick with southern French context.
rules.action: Consider Toulouse-area candidates and read street or institution names.
exceptions: Brick colour varies with lighting.
One orange-brick building is not city proof.

rules.observation: Granite walls/trim, dark slate roofs and gable-end chimneys in a coherent streetscape.
rules.action: Use Breton text or place names to separate Brittany from look-alikes.
exceptions: Granite and slate also occur in north-west Spain and Portugal.
Building stock and modern roofs vary.

rules.observation: Half-timbered houses with fish-scale roof tiles plus Germanic local names.
rules.action: Prioritise eastern France; resolve readable place names.
exceptions: Half-timbering also occurs in Normandy.
Names in -heim/-willer are more useful than half-timbering alone.

rules.observation: White Basque-style houses with timber framing painted red or green.
rules.action: Painted framing favours the French side; use karrika/kalea and local names to decide.
exceptions: Unpainted timber favours the Spanish side, but buildings cross these tendencies.
Basque language/flags alone do not resolve the country.

rules.observation: Extensive straight maritime-pine plantations on conspicuously flat sandy ground.
rules.action: Consider the Landes/Gironde area and corroborate with local text.
exceptions: Pines and sandy ground also occur in Iberia.
The flat plantation structure matters; pine species alone is weak.

rules.observation: Clearly identifiable eucalyptus stands in the scene.
rules.action: Use as a broad Iberian hint only after checking identification.
exceptions: Planting and ornamental trees can occur outside their common regions.
Never exclude France from a tree identification alone.
Vegetation, wetness and landscape appearance are correlated.

rules.observation: Canada is read as a Portuguese street-type word on a local address plaque.
rules.action: Prioritise Azorean candidates when the full address cannot be resolved directly.
exceptions: The source’s 99% figure concerns recorded addresses, not visible photographs.
A mention of the country Canada or a business name is not this clue.

rules.observation: Vereda or Entrada occurs as the street-type word in a Portuguese address.
rules.action: Consider Madeira after checking the full name in the gazetteer.
exceptions: Address-frequency statistics are not image probabilities.
A generic entrance label is not a street name.

rules.observation: An unresolved Portuguese locality begins Monte/Herdade, Casal/Casais or Cerro.
rules.action: Only after gazetteer lookup fails: Monte/Herdade favours Alentejo; Casal/Casais favours Lisboa/Santarém/Leiria; Cerro favours Algarve.
exceptions: The source samples address/locality records rather than visible signs.
A matched full name overrides the suffix/prefix tendency.
Do not convert the reported percentages/lifts into location probabilities.

rules.observation: An unresolved French place name has Plou-/Ker-/Tre-, -heim/-willer, -ville/-tot or -ac.
rules.action: Use Plou/Ker/Tre for Brittany; heim/willer for Alsace/Moselle; ville/tot for Normandy/north; ac for south-west or southern Brittany. Keep alternatives.
exceptions: Toponym patterns overlap and should follow full-name lookup.
The -ac pattern is not a south-east France rule.
A directional sign may name a distant locality.

workflow.action: Read full-resolution sign crops; retain raw text, confidence, alternatives and crop coordinates.
Resolve named places, postal codes, institution names, trail municipal codes and hunting-process areas.
Retrieve relevant rules by feature plus all surviving countries; include each rule’s exceptions.
Rerank candidates with capped evidence groups; compare maps/reference imagery for camera placement.
Ask about a visible unresolved separator only when the expected score gain justifies its penalty.
